t: LeetCode 1365 — How Many Numbers Are Smaller Than the Current Number
o: For each element in `nums`, we must count how many *other* elements are strictly smaller than it, and return these counts as an array. In Example 1 (`[8,1,2,2,3]`), 8 has four smaller values (1, 2, 2, 3), 1 has none, each 2 has one (just the 1), and 3 has three (1, 2, 2) — giving `[4,0,1,1,3]`. Example 3 shows duplicates of the maximum all get count 0. The constraints are tiny: n ≤ 500 and values in [0, 100], so even an O(n²) brute force passes easily; however, the small value range hints at a counting-sort-based O(n + k) solution where k = 101.
k: Brute force compares every pair — O(n²), fine for n ≤ 500.
Sorting lets us answer 'how many elements are smaller' via binary search or prefix positions.
Since values are bounded by 100, a frequency array with prefix sums gives counts in O(n + 101).

a.i: Directly translate the definition into code: for each index i, scan every other index j and increment a counter when nums[j] < nums[i]. This is exactly what the problem asks, requires no extra data structures, and is trivially correct. With n ≤ 500 it performs at most ~250k comparisons.
s: Create an answer array of length n.
For each i from 0 to n-1, initialize count = 0.
For each j != i, if nums[j] < nums[i], increment count.
Store count in answer[i] and return the array.
a.t: O(n²) — for each of n elements we scan all n elements.
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output array.

a.i: After sorting a copy of the array, all elements strictly smaller than x appear before the first occurrence of x. So the answer for x is simply the index of its first occurrence, found via binary search (lower bound). This reduces per-query cost to O(log n).
s: Copy and sort nums into sorted.
For each original element x, binary search for its lower-bound position p in sorted.
The answer is p (number of elements strictly less than x).
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; each of n lookups costs O(log n).

a.n: Approach 3: Counting Array with Prefix Sums (Optimal)
a.i: Values lie in [0, 100], so build a frequency table count[v] = number of occurrences of v. Then prefix[v] = number of elements ≤ v-1... more precisely, define prefix so that prefix[v] equals the number of elements strictly smaller than v: prefix[v] = prefix[v-1] + count[v-1]. Each query becomes O(1).
s: Build freq[0..101] counting occurrences of each value.
Compute prefix[v] = number of elements with value < v, via prefix[v] = prefix[v-1] + freq[v-1].
For each nums[i], answer is prefix[nums[i]].
a.t: O(n + k) where k = 101 — one pass to count, one pass over the fixed-size table, one pass to answer.
a.sp: O(k) = O(101) = O(1) extra space for the frequency/prefix table.

w: In an interview, start with brute force to confirm understanding, then mention sorting + binary search, and land on the counting-sort approach since the value range [0, 100] makes it clearly optimal. Common pitfalls: using ≤ instead of strict < when comparing, mishandling duplicates (all copies of a value share the same count), and forgetting that an element does not count itself (irrelevant here since x < x is false anyway). Edge cases: all-equal arrays (answer is all zeros) and arrays containing 0 (smallest possible value gets count 0). Likely follow-ups: what if values were unbounded (then sort + binary search wins), or if you needed counts of smaller-or-equal elements (adjust the prefix to include freq[v]).
